short.text: A khakhara deula has an oblong (rectangular) plan. Its roof is long and rounded on top, like half a barrel lying on its side.
short.note: N.K. Bose (1932): the ground plan of the khakhara 'is rectangular'. K.S. Behera: 'oblong bada and semi-cylindrical roof'. Mitra's ASI guide calls the roofs of its carved models 'wagon-vaulted'.

long.text: Two khakhara temples in Bhubaneswar are the Vaital Deul and the small Gauri temple.
The name khakhara comes from the kakharu, a kind of pumpkin-gourd. The temple's long, rounded roof looks a little like it.
long.note: Debala Mitra (1960): the name is 'due to the faint resemblance of the barrel-vaulted elongated roof of its temples with a variety of pumpkin-gourd, called kakharu in Oriya'. She links the local name vaitalu for this gourd with the name of the Vaital Deul.

long.text: This roof shape may copy very old halls, whose rounded roofs rested on timber or bent bamboo.
long.note: Debala Mitra (1960): the roof 'is a modified survival of the primitive halls with a semi-cylindrical roof resting on a framework of timber or bent split bamboos (in the case of a thatched roof)'.

long.text: Khakhara temples are often linked with the worship of goddesses. But goddesses are also found in temples of other types, and experts do not all agree about the Vaital Deul.
long.note: K.S. Behera (2005): the khakhara temple is 'used for Devi worship'. Debala Mitra (1960): the available evidence 'indicates that temples of this Order in Orissa belonged to the Sakta cult, though the converse is not true', as goddesses also sit in rekha temples such as the Mohini and Chitrakarini. Percy Brown (1959) calls the Vaital Deul 'a Siva temple of the Orissan group'.
N.K. Bose (1932): the type 'is limited to six examples in Bhubaneswar', but its miniatures are very common as decoration.
